claim: Msp1 is a conserved AAA ATPase in budding yeast localized to mitochondria.
source: Msp1 is a conserved AAA ATPase in budding yeast localized to mitochondria where it prevents accumulation of mistargeted tail-anchored (TA) proteins, including the peroxisomal TA protein Pex15.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work (Chen et al., 2014b; Okreglak and Walter, 2014) in the introduction.

claim: Msp1 prevents accumulation of mistargeted tail-anchored (TA) proteins at mitochondria.
source: Msp1 is a conserved AAA ATPase in budding yeast localized to mitochondria where it prevents accumulation of mistargeted tail-anchored (TA) proteins, including the peroxisomal TA protein Pex15.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work (Chen et al., 2014b; Okreglak and Walter, 2014).

claim: Pex15 is a peroxisomal TA protein that can be mistargeted to mitochondria.
source: Msp1 is a conserved AAA ATPase in budding yeast localized to mitochondria where it prevents accumulation of mistargeted tail-anchored (TA) proteins, including the peroxisomal TA protein Pex15.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work (Chen et al., 2014b; Okreglak and Walter, 2014).

claim: Msp1 also resides on peroxisomes.
source: Msp1 also resides on peroxisomes but it remains unknown how native TA proteins on mitochondria and peroxisomes evade Msp1 surveillance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work (Chen et al., 2014b; Okreglak and Walter, 2014) in the introduction.

claim: A small fraction of peroxisomal Pex15 is turned over by Msp1.
source: We found that a small fraction of peroxisomal Pex15, exaggerated by overexpression, is turned over by Msp1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Overexpression of Pex15 exaggerates Msp1-dependent turnover at peroxisomes.
source: We found that a small fraction of peroxisomal Pex15, exaggerated by overexpression, is turned over by Msp1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Pex15 molecules at mitochondria display age-independent Msp1 sensitivity.
source: Kinetic measurements guided by theoretical modeling revealed that Pex15 molecules at mitochondria display age-independent Msp1 sensitivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data and modeling in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Pex15 molecules at peroxisomes are rapidly converted from an initial Msp1-sensitive to an Msp1-resistant state.
source: By contrast, Pex15 molecules at peroxisomes are rapidly converted from an initial Msp1-sensitive to an Msp1-resistant state.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data and modeling in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Pex15 interacts with the peroxisomal membrane protein Pex3.
source: Lastly, we show that Pex15 interacts with the peroxisomal membrane protein Pex3, which shields Pex15 from Msp1-dependent turnover.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6A.

claim: Pex3 shields Pex15 from Msp1-dependent turnover.
source: Lastly, we show that Pex15 interacts with the peroxisomal membrane protein Pex3, which shields Pex15 from Msp1-dependent turnover.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Msp1 selects its substrates on the basis of their solitary membrane existence.
source: In sum, our work argues that Msp1 selects its substrates on the basis of their solitary membrane existence.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, based on inference from the experimental data showing that Pex3 binding protects Pex15 from Msp1.

claim: Tail-anchored (TA) proteins are integral membrane proteins with a single C-terminal transmembrane segment (TMS).
source: Tail-anchored (TA) proteins are integral membrane proteins with a single C-terminal transmembrane segment (TMS).
evidence: This is a definition stated in the introduction, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: The majority of TA proteins in S. cerevisiae are captured post-translationally by cytosolic factors of the conserved Guided Entry of TA proteins (GET) pathway.
source: In the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the majority of TA proteins are captured post-translationally by cytosolic factors of the conserved Guided Entry of TA proteins (GET) pathway, which deliver them to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane for insertion by a dedicated insertase (Denic et al., 2013; Hegde and Keenan, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work (Denic et al., 2013; Hegde and Keenan, 2011).

claim: The GET pathway delivers TA proteins to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane for insertion by a dedicated insertase.
source: In the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the majority of TA proteins are captured post-translationally by cytosolic factors of the conserved Guided Entry of TA proteins (GET) pathway, which deliver them to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane for insertion by a dedicated insertase (Denic et al., 2013; Hegde and Keenan, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work (Denic et al., 2013; Hegde and Keenan, 2011).

claim: TA proteins native to the outer mitochondrial and peroxisomal membranes are directly inserted into these membranes by mechanisms that are not well defined.
source: TA proteins native to the outer mitochondrial and peroxisomal membranes are directly inserted into these membranes by mechanisms that are not well defined (Chen et al., 2014a; Papić et al., 2013, and reviewed in Borgese and Fasana, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work (Chen et al., 2014a; Papić et al., 2013, and reviewed in Borgese and Fasana, 2011).

claim: Gene deletions of GET pathway components (getΔ) result in reduced cell growth.
source: Gene deletions of GET pathway components (getΔ) result in reduced cell growth, TA protein mistargeting to mitochondria, and cytosolic TA protein aggregates (Jonikas et al., 2009; Schuldiner et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work (Jonikas et al., 2009; Schuldiner et al., 2008).

claim: Gene deletions of GET pathway components (getΔ) result in TA protein mistargeting to mitochondria.
source: Gene deletions of GET pathway components (getΔ) result in reduced cell growth, TA protein mistargeting to mitochondria, and cytosolic TA protein aggregates (Jonikas et al., 2009; Schuldiner et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work (Jonikas et al., 2009; Schuldiner et al., 2008).

claim: Gene deletions of GET pathway components (getΔ) result in cytosolic TA protein aggregates.
source: Gene deletions of GET pathway components (getΔ) result in reduced cell growth, TA protein mistargeting to mitochondria, and cytosolic TA protein aggregates (Jonikas et al., 2009; Schuldiner et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work (Jonikas et al., 2009; Schuldiner et al., 2008).

claim: Two recent studies identified the ATPase associated with diverse cellular activities (AAA ATPase) Msp1 as an additional factor for supporting cell viability in the absence of GET pathway function.
source: Two recent studies identified the ATPase associated with diverse cellular activities (AAA ATPase) Msp1 as an additional factor for supporting cell viability in the absence of GET pathway function (Chen et al., 2014b; Okreglak and Walter, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work (Chen et al., 2014b; Okreglak and Walter, 2014).

claim: msp1Δ cells accumulate mislocalized TA proteins in the mitochondria.
source: Specifically, they observed that msp1Δ cells accumulate mislocalized TA proteins in the mitochondria and that double msp1Δ getΔ cells have synthetic sick genetic interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work (Chen et al., 2014b; Okreglak and Walter, 2014).

claim: Double msp1Δ getΔ cells have synthetic sick genetic interactions.
source: Specifically, they observed that msp1Δ cells accumulate mislocalized TA proteins in the mitochondria and that double msp1Δ getΔ cells have synthetic sick genetic interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work (Chen et al., 2014b; Okreglak and Walter, 2014).

claim: The sick phenotype of msp1Δ getΔ cells is associated with disruption of mitochondrial function.
source: This sick phenotype is associated with disruption of mitochondrial function and is exacerbated by overexpression of TA proteins prone to mislocalization (Chen et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to prior work (Chen et al., 2014b).

claim: The sick phenotype of msp1Δ getΔ cells is exacerbated by overexpression of TA proteins prone to mislocalization.
source: This sick phenotype is associated with disruption of mitochondrial function and is exacerbated by overexpression of TA proteins prone to mislocalization (Chen et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to prior work (Chen et al., 2014b).

claim: Msp1 is a cytosolically-facing transmembrane AAA ATPase.
source: Msp1 is a cytosolically-facing transmembrane AAA ATPase which resides on both mitochondria and peroxisomes (Chen et al., 2014b; Okreglak and Walter, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work (Chen et al., 2014b; Okreglak and Walter, 2014).

claim: Closely-related members of Msp1's AAA ATPase subfamily form hexamers that bind hydrophobic membrane substrates and use the energy of ATP hydrolysis to extract them from the membrane for protein degradation.
source: Closely-related members of Msp1's AAA ATPase subfamily form hexamers that bind hydrophobic membrane substrates and use the energy of ATP hydrolysis to extract them from the membrane for protein degradation (Olivares et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to prior work (Olivares et al., 2016).

claim: ATPase-dead mutations of Msp1 are unable to complement msp1Δ mutant phenotypes.
source: Several lines of evidence are consistent with the working model that Msp1 operates by a similar mechanism: ATPase-dead mutations of Msp1 are unable to complement msp1Δ mutant phenotypes; mitochondrial mistargeting of TA proteins leads to their enhanced co-immunoprecipitation with ATPase-dead Msp1; cells lacking Msp1 have increased half-lives of mistargeted TA proteins; and lastly, a complementary analysis of the mammalian Msp1 homolog ATAD1 (Chen et al., 2014b) established a conserved role for Msp1 in correcting errors in TA protein sorting.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to prior work (Chen et al., 2014b).

claim: Mitochondrial mistargeting of TA proteins leads to their enhanced co-immunoprecipitation with ATPase-dead Msp1.
source: Several lines of evidence are consistent with the working model that Msp1 operates by a similar mechanism: ATPase-dead mutations of Msp1 are unable to complement msp1Δ mutant phenotypes; mitochondrial mistargeting of TA proteins leads to their enhanced co-immunoprecipitation with ATPase-dead Msp1; cells lacking Msp1 have increased half-lives of mistargeted TA proteins; and lastly, a complementary analysis of the mammalian Msp1 homolog ATAD1 (Chen et al., 2014b) established a conserved role for Msp1 in correcting errors in TA protein sorting.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to prior work (Chen et al., 2014b).

claim: Cells lacking Msp1 have increased half-lives of mistargeted TA proteins.
source: Several lines of evidence are consistent with the working model that Msp1 operates by a similar mechanism: ATPase-dead mutations of Msp1 are unable to complement msp1Δ mutant phenotypes; mitochondrial mistargeting of TA proteins leads to their enhanced co-immunoprecipitation with ATPase-dead Msp1; cells lacking Msp1 have increased half-lives of mistargeted TA proteins; and lastly, a complementary analysis of the mammalian Msp1 homolog ATAD1 (Chen et al., 2014b) established a conserved role for Msp1 in correcting errors in TA protein sorting.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to prior work (Chen et al., 2014b).

claim: The mammalian Msp1 homolog ATAD1 has a conserved role in correcting errors in TA protein sorting.
source: Several lines of evidence are consistent with the working model that Msp1 operates by a similar mechanism: ATPase-dead mutations of Msp1 are unable to complement msp1Δ mutant phenotypes; mitochondrial mistargeting of TA proteins leads to their enhanced co-immunoprecipitation with ATPase-dead Msp1; cells lacking Msp1 have increased half-lives of mistargeted TA proteins; and lastly, a complementary analysis of the mammalian Msp1 homolog ATAD1 (Chen et al., 2014b) established a conserved role for Msp1 in correcting errors in TA protein sorting.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to prior work (Chen et al., 2014b).

claim: De novo Msp1 induction significantly enhanced mitochondrial YFP signal decay.
source: Starting with the same pre-existing mitochondrial Pex15 population, we found that de novo Msp1 induction significantly enhanced mitochondrial YFP signal decay (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Pex15ΔC30 is efficiently mistargeted to mitochondria because it lacks a C-terminal peroxisome targeting signal.
source: We reached a similar conclusion when we used a deletion variant of Pex15 (Pex15ΔC30) that is efficiently mistargeted to mitochondria because it lacks a C-terminal peroxisome targeting signal (Okreglak and Walter, 2014)(Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation to prior work (Okreglak and Walter, 2014) and experimental data in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Pex15ΔC30 was fully membrane-integrated prior to Msp1 induction.
source: To establish if Pex15ΔC30was fully membrane-integrated prior to Msp1 induction, we harvested cells after DOX treatment. Following cell lysis, we isolated crude mitochondria by centrifugation and treated them with Proteinase K (PK). Immunoblotting analysis against a C-terminal epitope engineered on Pex15 revealed the existence of a protected TMS-containing fragment that became PK-sensitive after solubilizing mitochondrial membranes with detergent (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by protease protection assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Msp1 can extract a fully-integrated substrate from the mitochondrial outer membrane.
source: Taken together, these findings argue that Msp1 can extract a fully-integrated substrate from the mitochondrial outer membrane and gave us a new tool for mechanistic dissection of Msp1 function in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results, based on inference from the experimental data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: β-estradiol enhanced YFP-Pex15 signal decay at punctate, non-mitochondrial structures.
source: While performing the previous analysis, we observed that β-estradiol also enhanced YFP-Pex15 signal decay at punctate, non-mitochondrial structures.
evidence: This is an observation stated in the results.

claim: The punctate structures with YFP-Pex15 signal correspond to peroxisomes.
source: To test if these punctae corresponded to peroxisomes, we used a strain with mCherry-marked peroxisomes (mCherry-PTS1) and induced YFP-Pex15 expression with a lower DOX concentration (10 μg/ml). Indeed, we saw robust YFP and mCherry signal co-localization with little apparent Pex15 mistargeting to mitochondria (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: β-estradiol-driven Msp1 expression enhanced YFP-Pex15 signal decay at peroxisomes.
source: As we initially surmised, β-estradiol-driven Msp1 expression enhanced YFP-Pex15 signal decay at peroxisomes (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: De novo induction of Msp1 activity enables degradation of peroxisomal Pex15.
source: Immunoblotting analysis of lysates prepared from comparably-treated cells provided further support for our conclusion that de novo induction of Msp1 activity enables degradation of peroxisomal Pex15 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Msp1-dependent turnover of peroxisomal Pex15 was the product of Pex15 overexpression.
source: To our knowledge, Msp1-induced turnover of peroxisomal Pex15 had not been reported previously. We found two pieces of evidence that this unexpected phenotype was the product of Pex15 overexpression.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results, based on inference from experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Treatment of pTET-YFP-PEX15 cells with 5 μg/ml DOX concentration induced a > 10 fold higher YFP fluorescence at peroxisomes relative to steady state levels of YFP-Pex15 expressed from its native promoter.
source: First, treatment of pTET-YFP-PEX15 cells with 5 μg/ml DOX concentration still induced a > 10 fold higher YFP fluorescence at peroxisomes relative to steady state levels of YFP-Pex15 expressed from its native promoter (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: There is no difference in natively-expressed peroxisomal Pex15 levels when comparing wild-type and msp1Δ cells.
source: Second, we could detect no difference in natively-expressed peroxisomal Pex15 levels when we compared wild-type and msp1Δ cells (Figure 3E, left panel).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E, left panel.

claim: Natively-expressed Pex15ΔC30 accumulates at mitochondria in msp1Δ cells.
source: This is unlikely a signal detection problem because we could robustly detect the accumulation of natively-expressed Pex15ΔC30 at mitochondria in msp1Δ cells (Figure 3E, right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E, right panel.

claim: Mitochondrial Pex15 turnover showed simple exponential decay.
source: Specifically, while mitochondrial Pex15 turnover showed simple exponential decay (i.e. linear decay after log-transformation), the decay of peroxisomal Pex15 appeared to be more complex, comprising faster and slower kinetic components.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data and modeling in Figure 4.

claim: The decay of peroxisomal Pex15 appeared to be more complex, comprising faster and slower kinetic components.
source: Specifically, while mitochondrial Pex15 turnover showed simple exponential decay (i.e. linear decay after log-transformation), the decay of peroxisomal Pex15 appeared to be more complex, comprising faster and slower kinetic components.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data and modeling in Figure 4.

claim: There are no major kinetic differences between Msp1 targeting to mitochondria and peroxisomes.
source: We detected no major kinetic differences between Msp1 targeting to mitochondria and peroxisomes that could explain this phenomenon (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C) but found a potential clue from a proteome-wide pulse-chase study showing that while most proteins decay exponentially, some exhibit non-exponential decay that can be explained by their stoichiometric excess over their binding partners (McShane et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Some proteins exhibit non-exponential decay that can be explained by their stoichiometric excess over their binding partners.
source: We detected no major kinetic differences between Msp1 targeting to mitochondria and peroxisomes that could explain this phenomenon (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C) but found a potential clue from a proteome-wide pulse-chase study showing that while most proteins decay exponentially, some exhibit non-exponential decay that can be explained by their stoichiometric excess over their binding partners (McShane et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation to prior work (McShane et al., 2016).

claim: Peroxisomal membranes have unique residents that interact with native Pex15.
source: Since peroxisomal membranes have unique residents that interact with native Pex15 (Eckert and Johnsson, 2003), we hypothesized that non-exponential decay of overexpressed peroxisomal Pex15 arises due to the existence of an Msp1-sensitive 'solitary' Pex15 state and an Msp1-insensitive 'partner-bound' Pex15 state.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation to prior work (Eckert and Johnsson, 2003).

claim: Non-exponential decay of overexpressed peroxisomal Pex15 arises due to the existence of an Msp1-sensitive 'solitary' Pex15 state and an Msp1-insensitive 'partner-bound' Pex15 state.
source: Since peroxisomal membranes have unique residents that interact with native Pex15 (Eckert and Johnsson, 2003), we hypothesized that non-exponential decay of overexpressed peroxisomal Pex15 arises due to the existence of an Msp1-sensitive 'solitary' Pex15 state and an Msp1-insensitive 'partner-bound' Pex15 state.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the results, based on inference from experimental data and prior work.

claim: Mitochondria are unlikely to have Pex15-binding partners.
source: By contrast, since mitochondria are unlikely to have Pex15-binding partners, mitochondrial Pex15 would exist in an obligate solitary state and would therefore decay exponentially.
evidence: This is stated in the results as part of the hypothesis, based on inference.

claim: Mitochondrial Pex15 would exist in an obligate solitary state and would therefore decay exponentially.
source: By contrast, since mitochondria are unlikely to have Pex15-binding partners, mitochondrial Pex15 would exist in an obligate solitary state and would therefore decay exponentially.
evidence: This is stated in the results as part of the hypothesis, based on inference.

claim: The 1-state model and 2-state models were indistinguishable for mitochondrial Msp1 substrate turnover.
source: In both the presence and absence of Msp1, our measurements could be similarly explained by both 1-state and 2-state models. The fits from these two models were almost identical (Figure 4C–D, Figure 4G, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by model fitting data shown in Figure 4C–D, Figure 4G, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Msp1 enhances Pex15 clearance from mitochondria as part of a simple exponential process.
source: Thus, we parsimoniously concluded that Msp1 enhances Pex15 clearance from mitochondria as part of a simple exponential process.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results, based on inference from model fitting data.

claim: The 1-state and 2-state models were indistinguishable in the absence of Msp1 for peroxisomal Pex15.
source: We again found that the 1-state model and 2-state were indistinguishable in the absence of Msp1.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by model fitting data shown in Figure 4E–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Pex15 in the nascent state decayed ~4 fold faster than Pex15 in the mature state.
source: The fit parameters from the 2-state model, which more closely approximated measured Pex15 turnover, revealed that Pex15 in the nascent state decayed ~4 fold faster (kdecay, 1 = 3.45 hr−1) than Pex15 in the mature state (kdecay, 2 = 0.87 hr−1) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by model fitting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the 1-state model, transient Msp1 overexpression in cells with constitutive Pex15 expression should equally destabilize all Pex15 molecules, thus rapidly reducing their mean age over time.
source: Specifically, in the 1-state model, transient Msp1 overexpression in cells with constitutive Pex15 expression should equally destabilize all Pex15 molecules, thus rapidly reducing their mean age over time (Figure 5B, top left panel).
evidence: This is a prediction stated in the results, based on theoretical modeling shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the 2-state model, Pex15 age should be buffered against Msp1 overexpression because of two opposing forces.
source: By contrast, in the 2-state model, Pex15 age should be buffered against Msp1 overexpression because of two opposing forces (Figure 4B and Figure 5B, top right panel): At one end, there would be an increase in kdecay,1 leading to less nascent Pex15, which would drive down the mean age over time. However, there would also be an opposing consequence of rapid depletion of new peroxisomal Pex15 by Msp1: the mature population of Pex15 would receive fewer new (younger) molecules, which would drive up the mean age over time.
evidence: This is a prediction stated in the results, based on theoretical modeling shown in Figure 4B and Figure 5B.

claim: Both models predict that transient Msp1 expression would result in a decrease in peroxisomal Pex15 levels, albeit with differing kinetics.
source: Notably, both models predict that transient Msp1 expression would result in a decrease in peroxisomal Pex15 levels, albeit with differing kinetics (Figure 5B, bottom panels).
evidence: This is a prediction stated in the results, based on theoretical modeling shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The peroxisomal mCherry:sfYFP fluorescence ratio was insensitive to β-estradiol treatment.
source: More strikingly, the peroxisomal mCherry:sfYFP fluorescence ratio was insensitive to β-estradiol treatment, consistent with the prediction of the 2-state model (Figure 5B–C, top panels).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B–C, top panels.

claim: There is a Pex15 maturation process at peroxisomes that converts newly-synthesized Pex15 molecules from an Msp1-sensitive to an Msp1-insensitive state.
source: Collectively, our experimental evidence and theoretical analysis strongly support the existence of a Pex15 maturation process at peroxisomes that converts newly-synthesized Pex15 molecules from an Msp1-sensitive to an Msp1-insensitive state.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results, based on inference from experimental data and theoretical modeling in Figure 5.

claim: The cytosolic AAA proteins Pex1 and Pex6 form a ternary complex with Pex15.
source: The cytosolic AAA proteins Pex1 and Pex6 are two prime candidates for testing this hypothesis because they form a ternary complex with Pex15 (Birschmann et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation to prior work (Birschmann et al., 2003).

claim: There is no decrease in YFP-Pex15 levels in pex1Δ or pex6Δ cells.
source: However, we did not observe the expected decrease in YFP-Pex15 levels in pex1Δ or pex6Δ cells that would be indicative of enhanced turnover by Msp1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The Pex1/6/15 complex is a regulator of peroxisome destruction by selective autophagy.
source: To look for additional Pex15 binding partners, we noted that the Pex1/6/15 complex is a regulator of peroxisome destruction by selective autophagy (Kamber et al., 2015; Nuttall et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations to prior work (Kamber et al., 2015; Nuttall et al., 2014).

claim: Selective autophagy of peroxisomes is initiated by Atg36, a receptor protein bound to the peroxisomal membrane protein Pex3.
source: This process is initiated by Atg36, a receptor protein bound to the peroxisomal membrane protein Pex3 (Motley et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation to prior work (Motley et al., 2012).

claim: Pex15 interacts with Pex3 by co-immunoprecipitation analysis.
source: Consistent with a previously published split-ubiquitin assay for detecting protein-protein interactions (Eckert and Johnsson, 2003), we found that Pex15 interacts with Pex3 by co-immunoprecipitation analysis (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Pex3 is essential for targeting of numerous peroxisomal membrane proteins.
source: Specifically, Pex3 is essential for targeting of numerous peroxisomal membrane proteins, which is why pex3Δ cells lack functional peroxisomes (Fang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation to prior work (Fang et al., 2004).

claim: pex3Δ cells lack functional peroxisomes.
source: Specifically, Pex3 is essential for targeting of numerous peroxisomal membrane proteins, which is why pex3Δ cells lack functional peroxisomes (Fang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation to prior work (Fang et al., 2004).

claim: Pex3 is normally turned over very slowly.
source: Since Pex3 is normally turned over very slowly (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and Belle et al., 2006), promoter shut-off is not a suitable method for acutely depleting Pex3.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and citation to prior work (Belle et al., 2006).

claim: Auxin addition induced rapid Pex3 destruction, which was dependent on OsTir1 expression and independent of Msp1.
source: Immunoblotting analysis for the V5 epitope revealed that Auxin addition induced rapid Pex3 destruction, which was dependent on OsTir1 expression and independent of Msp1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–E.

claim: Peroxisomes persisted for hours following Pex3 destruction.
source: Importantly, microscopic analysis of cells co-expressing Pex3-GFP-AID and mCherry-PTS1 revealed that peroxisomes persisted for hours following Pex3 destruction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pex3 degradation immediately increased the rate of Msp1-dependent Pex15 turnover.
source: Strikingly, we observed that Pex3 degradation immediately increased the rate of Msp1-dependent Pex15 turnover (Figure 6C), thus unmasking endogenous Pex15 as a latent substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Endogenous Pex15 is a latent substrate for Msp1.
source: Strikingly, we observed that Pex3 degradation immediately increased the rate of Msp1-dependent Pex15 turnover (Figure 6C), thus unmasking endogenous Pex15 as a latent substrate.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results, based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Pex3 degradation did not result in Msp1-dependent destabilization of Pex11 and Pex12.
source: By contrast, Pex3 degradation did not result in Msp1-dependent destabilization of Pex11 and Pex12, two peroxisomal membrane proteins we analyzed as controls for the substrate specificity of Msp1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I–J).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1I–J.

claim: Constitutive overexpression of Pex3 from the strong TDH3 promoter blunted the effect of de novo Msp1 induction on transiently overexpressed YFP-Pex15.
source: Consistent with this idea, constitutive overexpression of Pex3 from the strong TDH3 promoter blunted the effect of de novo Msp1 induction on transiently overexpressed YFP-Pex15 (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D–E.

claim: Pex3 stoichiometrically protects Pex15 from Msp1 recognition at peroxisomes.
source: Taken together, these data argue that Pex3 stoichiometrically protects Pex15 from Msp1 recognition at peroxisomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results, based on inference from experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: GFP fused to the TMS of the mammalian Msp1 homolog ATAD1 is targeted to both mitochondria and peroxisomes.
source: A recent study showed that GFP fused to the TMS of the mammalian Msp1 homolog ATAD1 is targeted to both mitochondria and peroxisomes (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation to prior work (Liu et al., 2016).

claim: The TMS of Msp1 is an ambiguous targeting signal whose function is to localize the rest of Msp1 into proximity with its substrates.
source: This suggests that the TMS of Msp1 is an ambiguous targeting signal whose function is to localize the rest of Msp1 into proximity with its substrates.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results, based on inference from prior work (Liu et al., 2016).

claim: Tom70TMS-Msp1-YFP produced from the MSP1 promoter is primarily localized to mitochondria with some residual localization to peroxisomes.
